title: The scheme-theoretic normalizer of a Borel subgroup
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic derived subgroups eventually become trivial, where the derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. A Borel subgroup is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. Let $G$ be smooth and connected and let $B\subseteq G$ be a Borel subgroup. For every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and every $g\in G(A)$, if $g_{A\prime}B(A\prime)g_{A\prime}^{-1}=B(A\prime)$ for every commutative $A$-algebra $A\prime$, then $g\in B(A)$. Thus the normalizer subgroup functor $N_G(B)$ equals $B$ on all test algebras, including nonreduced ones. No reductivity hypothesis is imposed on $G$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48 (Normalizer Theorem), printed p.367, with the normalizer scheme of Lemma 17.47, printed p.366. The equality is scheme-theoretic, not just an equality on F-points.

proof.text: We prove the stated functor equality by strong induction on $d=\dim G$, simultaneously for every smooth connected affine group of dimension $d$ over the fixed algebraically closed field and every Borel in it. If $B=G$, the conclusion is immediate, so assume $B\ne G$. Choose a maximal torus $T\subseteq B$ which is maximal in $G$ by [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy]. By [lem-sfb-maximal-torus-centralizer-borel], $C_G(T)\subseteq B$. Apply [lem-sfb-cartan-containing-normalizer-smooth] with $H=B$: the normalizer functor is represented by a smooth closed affine finite-type subgroup $N\subseteq G$. It remains to show $N(F)\subseteq B(F)$; the passage from this inclusion to equality on arbitrary algebras is carried out in the last step.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, first two paragraphs, printed p.367. Strong induction includes dimension zero; the argument below either closes directly or invokes a strictly smaller dimension.

proof.text: Fix $x\in N(F)$. The tori $T$ and $xTx^{-1}$ are maximal in the smooth connected group $B$. Apply the conjugacy assertion of [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] to $B$: choose $b\in B(F)$ with $b(xTx^{-1})b^{-1}=T$. Replace $x$ by $bx$. This replacement preserves membership in $N(F)$, and proving $bx\in B(F)$ proves the original assertion. We may therefore assume $xTx^{-1}=T$. The morphism $\varphi:T\to T$, $t\mapsto xtx^{-1}t^{-1}$, is a homomorphism: on every test algebra its two factors take values in the commutative group $T$, and expanding $\varphi(t_1t_2)$ gives $\varphi(t_1)\varphi(t_2)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, third paragraph and displayed commutator homomorphism, printed p.367.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-torus-endomorphism-kernel-dichotomy] to $\varphi$. First suppose its kernel contains $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^s$ with $s\geq1$. Then $x$ commutes with $S$ after every scalar extension. Put $C=C_G(S)$, smooth and connected by [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected]. Since $S\subseteq T\subseteq B$, the existing [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-borel-intersection] applies to $(G,B,S)$: the scheme-theoretic intersection $D=C\times_G B$ is a Borel of $C$. Since $x\in C(F)$ and conjugation by $x$ preserves $B$, it preserves $D$ as a subgroup scheme.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, non-surjective commutator case, printed p.367.

The induction hypothesis for the smooth connected group $C$ and its Borel $D$ therefore gives $x\in D(F)\subseteq B(F)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, first induction branch, printed p.367.

proof.text: If $C=G$, then $S$ is central in $G$. Form $q:G\to J=G/S$ using [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]; $J$ is smooth connected affine of finite type. By [lem-sfb-quotient-borel-torus-images], $E=q(B)$ is a Borel of $J$, and $B\to E$ is faithfully flat. Its inverse image is exactly $B$: a test point in $q^{-1}(E)$ lifts locally to a point of $B$ with the same image, and their ratio lies in $S\subseteq B$; membership in the closed subgroup $B$ descends because its defining ideal vanishes faithfully flat locally only if it vanishes. Moreover $\dim J=\dim G-s<\dim G$. To check the dimension formula, use the left translation action of $G$ on $J$ and [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry]: the orbit map at $q(e)$ is the surjective map $q$, the orbit is all of $J$, which is reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], and its stabilizer is $S$. Thus the orbit dimension formula gives the displayed equality. Since $x$ normalizes $B$, $q(x)$ normalizes its image $E$ (check after local lifts along $B\to E$). Induction applied to $(J,E)$ gives $q(x)\in E(F)$, whence $x\in q^{-1}(E)(F)=B(F)$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, central-torus quotient induction branch, printed p.367; Proposition 1.66 for the quotient dimension formula.

proof.text: It remains to treat the case that $\varphi:T\to T$ is faithfully flat. By [lem-sfb-chevalley-scheme-line-stabilizer], choose a finite-dimensional rational $G$-representation $V$ and a line $L=Fv$, $v\ne0$, whose scheme-theoretic stabilizer is $N$. The action on this line is a character $\chi:N\to\mathbf G_m$. Because $x,T\subseteq N$, the identity $\chi(xtx^{-1}t^{-1})=1$ holds on every test algebra. Faithful flatness of $\varphi$ implies that $\chi|_T=1$: its coordinate functions become those of the constant map after the injective pullback along $\varphi$. In particular $T$ fixes $v$. The character here is a character of $N$, not an assumed character of $G$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, surjective commutator case, printed p.367; Theorem 4.27 for the line stabilizer.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] to $B$ and let $U$ be its smooth connected unipotent normal subgroup with torus quotient $p:B\to B/U$. By [lem-sfb-solvable-torus-complements], $p|_T$ is an isomorphism. For every test point $b$ set $t=(p|_T)^{-1}p(b)$ and $u=bt^{-1}$; then $u\in U$, so $b=ut$. The restriction $\chi|_U$ is trivial by [lem-sfb-unipotent-to-multiplicative-trivial]. Together with $\chi|_T=1$, this shows that $B$ fixes $v$ on every test algebra.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, B fixes the vector, printed p.367; Theorem 16.33 for the solvable decomposition.

proof.text: Obtain the quotient $\pi:G\to Q=G/B$ from [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homogeneous-quotient]. It is an fpqc covering, and [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry] makes $Q$ proper and geometrically integral, hence nonempty connected and reduced. The orbit morphism $a:G\to V$, $g\mapsto gv$, has equal pullbacks to $G\times_QG$: a pair there is $(g,gb)$ for $b\in B$, and $gbv=gv$ by the previous step. Consequently it descends to $\bar a:Q\to V$ by [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent]. By [lem-weil-pbc-proper-reduced-algclosed-global-sections-product], $\Gamma(Q,\mathcal O_Q)=F$. Each coordinate of $\bar a$ is therefore constant, with value its value at $\pi(e)$, so $\bar a$ is the constant morphism $v$. Thus $G$ fixes $v$ scheme-theoretically, and hence stabilizes $L$; the defining property of $L$ gives $G\subseteq N$, or $G=N$.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, complete connected quotient forces constant orbit, printed p.367; A.75(g).

proof.text: Now $B$ is normal in $G$ since $G=N$. By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], the same quotient $Q=G/B$ is affine: the quotient there and $Q$ agree by their coset and local-lift descriptions (define the maps after local lifts; [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-representable-descent] glues them and their inverse identities). The preceding step gives $\Gamma(Q,\mathcal O_Q)=F$, so the affine scheme $Q$ is $\operatorname{Spec}F$. Since the kernel of $G\to G/B$ is $B$, this implies $G=B$, and in particular $x\in B(F)$. This closes the surjective branch without appealing to a normal-Borel corollary. Every induction use above has strictly smaller dimension, and the other branches close without induction, so strong induction proves $N(F)\subseteq B(F)$ in all dimensions, including zero.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, final assertion, printed p.367; agent expansion via proper affine quotient in place of the citation to 17.33(b).

proof.text: Finally let $I$ be the ideal cutting out $B$ in the affine finite-type scheme $N$. Smoothness of $N$ makes its coordinate algebra reduced by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]. Every $f\in I$ vanishes at every $F$-point of $N$, because all these points lie in $B(F)$. By [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing], $f=0$. Hence $I=0$ and $N=B$ as schemes, not merely on field points. Evaluating their representing functors on an arbitrary commutative $F$-algebra $A$ gives the requested implication. Conversely every point of $B(A)$ normalizes $B$ after every extension by the group laws, so the two subgroup functors are equal.

source.place: Theorem 17.48, smoothness reduction and final scheme-theoretic conclusion, printed p.367.

lean.statement: theorem borelGroupScheme_normalizer_iff {F : Type u} [Field F] [IsAlgClosed F] (G B : Over (Spec (.of F))) [GrpObj G] [GrpObj B] [IsAffine G.left] [LocallyOfFiniteType G.hom] [QuasiCompact G.hom] [Smooth G.hom] [ConnectedSpace G.left] (i : B ⟶ G) (hB : IsBorelGroupScheme i) (A : CommAlgCat.{u} F) (g : (algSpec (.of F)).obj (op A) ⟶ G) : (∀ (A' : CommAlgCat.{u} F) (f : A ⟶ A'), Set.range (fun b : (algSpec (.of F)).obj (op A') ⟶ B ↦ ((algSpec (.of F)).map f.op ≫ g) * (b ≫ i) * ((algSpec (.of F)).map f.op ≫ g)⁻¹) = Set.range (fun b : (algSpec (.of F)).obj (op A') ⟶ B ↦ b ≫ i)) ↔ ∃ b : (algSpec (.of F)).obj (op A) ⟶ B, b ≫ i = g

The ↔ renders the node's N_G(B)=B clause, and the converse is true because IsClosedSubgroupScheme extends IsMonHom. No extra assumptions; universes are uniform in u.
